---
title: "Airhouse"
description: "Oxygen's managed warehouse, where your data lands and is queried from"
---

**Airhouse** is Oxygen's managed warehouse, the place where your data lands
and where the [semantic model](/guide/build/semantic-model/simple-model) and
agents query it from. It speaks the Postgres wire protocol, so any
Postgres-compatible client or BI tool can connect, and it runs every query on
[DuckDB](https://duckdb.org) over tables stored with
[DuckLake](https://ducklake.select). It has three parts:

- The **data plane** accepts connections and checks every statement, first
  the password, then the caller's role and limits, before DuckDB runs it.
- The **control plane** creates databases and users, and mints the
  short-lived credentials that every connection uses.
- **Storage** holds each database's catalog in Postgres and its table data as
  Parquet files in object storage, isolated from every other database.

## Why a warehouse per workspace

Most warehouses are shared infrastructure guarded by long-lived service
passwords. Those passwords end up in config files and CI secrets, they are
rarely rotated, and one leaked key can read everything. Airhouse inverts this
in two ways.

- **No long-lived keys.** Agents, pipelines, and apps never hold a warehouse
  password. Each time one needs to connect, Oxygen mints a credential that
  expires on its own, carrying only the role the caller is entitled to.
- **Isolation by default.** Each workspace gets its own Airhouse database, with
  its own catalog, its own storage location, its own users, and its own query
  limits, so one workspace can't see another's data and each one's load
  can be capped on its own.

Because tables are stored as standard Parquet with a DuckLake catalog, the
data is never locked into Airhouse: it stays readable with DuckDB and DuckLake
tooling.

## The data plane

Every connection names its database with the standard Postgres `database`
parameter. The data plane verifies the credential, opens an isolated DuckDB
session with that database's catalog attached, and then checks each statement
against the caller's role (`reader`, `writer`, or `admin`) and the database's
rate and concurrency limits. Statements that fail a check never reach the
engine. DuckDB reads only the Parquet files and columns a query needs, and
results stream back in the Postgres wire format.

## The control plane

When Airhouse is enabled for a workspace, Oxygen provisions a database for it
through the control plane. From then on, Oxygen mints credentials on demand,
and the role each credential carries follows your organization role: owners
get `admin`, admins get `writer`, and members get `reader`. This is how
[Airway](/guide/build/data-infrastructure/airway) pipelines load data and how
[custom apps](/guide/build/sdk/functions) append their own facts without ever
holding a password.

## Storage

Each database's catalog, which records its schemas, tables, data files, and
snapshots, lives in Postgres. Its table data lives as Parquet files under its
own prefix in S3-compatible object storage. Every write is an atomic commit
that creates a new snapshot, so readers always see a consistent view, and
earlier snapshots stay queryable with
[time travel](/airhouse/guides/tables-and-storage#snapshots-and-time-travel).

## When to use Airhouse

Use Airhouse when you want Oxygen to manage the warehouse for you. It is
where Airway pipelines land extracted data and where custom apps append their
own facts. If you already have a warehouse, you do not need Airhouse, since
Oxygen [connects to your own](/guide/build/connect-data) and the semantic
model compiles the same way regardless of where the data lives.
